title: Catherine of Siena
hookLine: a dyer's daughter who told popes what to do and nursed the plague-sick
carry: be who god meant you to be
last: A LOVE BIGGER THAN THE HURT.

cards: A letter opens warmly, calling its reader father. A few lines later it tells him, plainly, that he is failing and needs to be braver. The reader is the pope.
The writer is a young woman from Siena, in Italy, with no title, no money and no official role. Nobody appointed her to advise the pope. She did it anyway.
And between letters, she was nursing the plague-sick and burying the dead. Today: Catherine Benincasa.

teach.b: Catherine was the daughter of a wool dyer in Siena, one of the youngest of a very large family; tradition says more than twenty children. As a girl she decided to give her whole life to God.

Her family pushed back hard, wanting her married. She refused. She didn't join a convent; she joined a group of lay women connected to the Dominican order, and lived at home, in a little room, praying.
Then, in her twenties, she went out.

She cared for the sick and the poor of Siena, and when plague came back, she nursed the dying and buried the dead. People gathered around her, friars, nobles, ordinary people, calling her mamma. And she spoke up.
The popes then lived not in Rome but in Avignon, in France.
Catherine was convinced the pope belonged in Rome. She told him so in letter after letter, and even traveled to Avignon to say it in person.
The pope did return to Rome; historians still debate how much she influenced that. Tradition says she learned to write only late; she dictated most of her letters to friends.
A well-known saying of hers is on posters and mugs: be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire. Those exact words aren't hers.
They're a loose modern version of a letter telling a friend that if he were what he ought to be, he'd set all Italy on fire. But the idea is truly hers. She died at thirty-three.
In 1970 the Catholic Church named her a Doctor of the Church. Her boldness came from prayer, and it went out as love.

how: Catholics honor Catherine as a saint and Doctor of the Church, with a feast day on April 29, and Christians of other churches read her letters and her book, The Dialogue, as models of prayer that turns into bold action.

games.q: you're a young woman with no title, and you believe the pope belongs in Rome, not Avignon. what do you do?
o: write to him, again and again, and go to see him.
keep quiet; it's not your place.
games.why: she wrote letter after letter and traveled to Avignon. the pope did return to Rome, though historians debate how much she influenced it.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've kept quiet about that might need saying, to a friend, a boss, a family member, a group: not a rant, one honest sentence said with love.
Picture saying it the way Catherine began her letters, warmly, and then clearly, and notice any fear, and any care underneath it. If you pray, you can ask for courage and kindness together.
